# **What is the problem represented to be in China's world-class ** **university policy? A poststructural analysis**
Etienne Woo
Faculty of Education, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK
### **ABSTRACT**
Underlying current research on China's world-class university (WCU) policy approaches are analytical foci that privilege the agency of social actors and the problem-solving approach to policy analysis. Foucauldian poststructuralists draw our attention to policy document, which is seen as a discourse that organizes and administers society. Inspired by Foucault, Carol Bacchi's 'What's the Problem Represented to Be?' approach (WPR) views policy document as a technology of governmentality. As proposed solutions to a problem, policy text produces the very problem that it seeks to address. Carol Bacchi draws our analytical attention to the rationalities, technologies of governing and subjectification effects created by particular problem representations in the WCU policy. Using WPR, this paper shows that WCU is represented as merely a technical, managerial and organizational problem. Such representations naturally reify WCU in material terms, such as research output, and in a temporal form of state planning. Genealogically, the root of WCU can be traced to the neoliberal movement of knowledge economy. However, Shanghai Ranking overturned this centerperiphery landscape in disseminating the concept of WCU. China's one-party state means that WCU is pursued at the expense of sacrificing social sciences and subjecting academics and students to become 'red experts.'
### **ARTICLE HISTORY **
Received 20 August 2021 Accepted 16 February 2022
### **KEYWORDS **
Chinese higher education; Chinese world-class universities; poststructural discourse analysis; WPR approach
## **Introduction**
Altbach [(2004,](#page-18-0) 20) wrote: 'Everyone wants a world-class university. No country feels it can do without one.' China has ultimately been able to acquire one. On 18 September 2020 an expert panel unanimously proclaimed that: 'Tsinghua University has comprehensively completed the task of building a double first-classes (world first-class university and first-class disciplines) university of high quality; the quality of education it offers and its impact on society and international reputation has been continuously rising, it has thus become an all-round world-class university' (Tsinghua University News [2020](#page-21-0)). This self-certification tells us two interesting pieces of information: 1) not being a world-class university (hereafter, WCU) was a 'problem' for Tsinghua University (and, of course, for China, too); 2) the 'problem' is now solved.
China's WCU pursuit is a top-design national policy, generously funded by central and provincial governments (Huang 2015, 213). The Chinese government launched the '211' and '985' projects in 1995 and 1998, respectively. The former aimed to develop 100 leading universities domestically by the early 21st century, and the latter aimed to promote the development and reputation of Chinese higher education by elevating some elite universities to world-class status in the 21st century. The State Council's 2003-2007 Education Revitalization Action Plan had already hailed building WCU as a strategy for 'enhancing the comprehensive strength of higher education and improving China's international competitiveness' (Ministry of Education [hereafter, MOE], 2004, second article). Eventually, in 2015, China unveiled its most comprehensive WCU policy, known as World First-Class University and First-Class Academic Discipline Construction Plan (commonly known as the double first-class plan). Out of the 3,005 higher education institutions in China, a total of 42 universities were designated as would-be WCUs in China's double first-class plan.<sup>2</sup> (Thirty-six universities were classified as Category A, while six were classified as the less prestigious Category B.)
Chinese WCU policies were formulated with a common unifying purpose of solving a presupposed problem - the lack of WCUs in China. This problem-solving approach reflects the general policy thinking in WCU research. It is believed that there is a formula for a world-class university if the right 'ingredients' (Crew 2019) are in place or a roadmap (Tayeb, Zahed, and Ritzen 2016) is well executed in acquiring the correct characteristics of WCU (Salmi 2009). This study challenges the problem-solving view of policy research.
We need to reflect on where the thinking that involves problem solving comes from and the political implications of a particular model of problem-solving thinking (Bacchi 2020). A Foucault-inspired poststructural analysis views problem solving as 'governing knowledge', which organizes and administers our society (Bacchi 2020, 84). Poststructuralists suggest a shift away from problem-solving analysis in policymaking to focus on how society is governed by the very problems that policies seek to solve. It represents a change of analytical focus from governing to governmentality. Carol Bacchi's 'What is the problem represented to be?' approach (WPR) is a Foucault-inspired poststructural discourse analysis tool for policy analysis. WPR sees policy documents as 'levers' that 'open up reflections on the forms of governing and associated effects, instituted through a particular way of constituting a "problem" (Bacchi and Goodwin 2016, 18). Taking an WPR approach to investigate WCU policy encourages researchers not only to move away from 'functionalist, rational, and scientific models' that have tended to 'operate within a traditionalistic (i.e. positivist) paradigm' (Diem et al. 2014, 1068), but also allows them to reflect upon why and how certain facets of the WCU policy make it to the political agenda and the ways in which 'problems' get represented and hence produced in the policy. Employing WPR as a policy analysis tool, this study aims to answer the following broad and nested question: how is the 'problem' of WCU in terms of rationalities, technologies of power and subjectification effects - constructed in the policy text?
### **Education policymaking in China**
China's WCU policy is the culmination of many years of ongoing efforts of state-led higher education internationalization. Putting WCU policy in the broader context of internationalization, this review seeks briefly to delineate the evolution of WCU policymaking in the context of Chinese higher education internationalization, which has epitomized the problem-solving thinking processes.
#### *State perspective: antidotes to backward development and lack of international * *status*
Analyzing extensive internationalization policies since 1949, Zheng and Kapoor divided higher education development into three periods (1949–1976, 1997–2002, 2003–2019) and demonstrated that internationalization could be understood as part of an ongoing process of state formation, in relation to national and global developments during key stages of China's development (Zheng and Kapoor [2021](#page-21-1)). Similarly, after tracking Chinese education policies from 2001 to 2017, three rationales were identified in internationalizing Chinese universities: economic modernization, build-up of human capital, and catching up with the West (Li [2017)](#page-19-5). In the pre-reform era (1949–1978), internationalization took the form of Sovietization in Chinese higher education, thereby establishing technical universities, which were ministry-supervised specialized research institutes. From 1978, when China introduced economic reform, up to the late 1990s, the internationalization emphasis was to learn from the West in the form of human capital – be it sending government-sponsored students overseas or establishing jointdegree programs between Chinese and foreign universities within China. Since the late 1990s, there was also a subtle tilt from learning from the West to strengthening the research capacity of domestic elite universities for further economic development in an increasingly integrated global economy. After China surpassed Japan and became the second-largest economy in 2010, having a number of world-class universities not only was commensurate with China's growing economic might and geopolitical influence, but also sat well within the narrative of turning the country into a 'modern socialist nation' by 2031 and a 'prosperous' and 'strong' one – a global leader on par with the US – by 2049 (Nakazawa [2017)](#page-20-2). The periodization of higher education policies seems to suggest that not only there is a solution to a preidentified problem in a policy for different stages of China's transformations, but also that the policy changes are driven by changes in domestic and global contexts. More attention should be paid to ways in which problems are created in a policy and how the policy thereby become a tool of for population's self-governing. Although both Sovietization and WCU are emulations with the aim of fueling China's economic growth, the former produces the problem as the lack of resources and personnel concertation in higher education whereas the latter produces the problem as catching up with research-intensive universities in the West. In turn, people in higher education were governed by a drive to achieve a teleological end during Sovietization, while steering by the state and self-government of individuals are prevalent in the pursuit of WCU.

#### *Institutional perspective: not Western enough as a 'problem'*
Chinese flagship universities consciously and voluntarily absorbed the Western elite university model (mainly Anglo-Saxon) as a reference in their institutional policymaking when they were pushed on the global higher education landscape (Pan [2006](#page-20-3)). Since the mid-1990s, elite Chinese universities have begun adopting the eight characteristics of the emerging global model of research universities: transcending national boundaries, research-intensiveness, new roles for faculty members, worldwide recruitment of staff and students, diversified sources of funding, global cooperation, new forms of relationships with stakeholders, and greater internal complexity (Mohrman, Ma, and Baker [2008](#page-20-4), 7). Policymaking at the institutional levels closely reflected the global rise of neoliberalism in higher education, which values 'efficiency, deliverability, and performance, and encourages competition, excellence, and high rates of return' (Zhang [2018,](#page-21-2) p. i). The two internationalization strategies adopted by Tsinghua University were 'injecting an international dimension to campus experience' and 'projecting itself out into the world' (Wang and Seddon [2014](#page-21-3), 33). Chinese universities have introduced requirements or incentives for academics to publish in well-known English-language journals because institutional policymakers believe such publications can increase the international exposure of universities and broaden international cooperation and exchange as well (Xu [2020](#page-21-4)). International standards in research excellence, international faculty hiring, student recruitment, transnational cooperation, and domestic technology transfer are among the main policy changes adopted by the aspiring flagship Chinese universities (Yang and Welch [2012](#page-21-5)). Impacted by the policies aiming to move China from the periphery to the center of global higher education, faculties also have to adjust their daily work routine, their perception of scholarship, the ways they teach (for example, using English as the medium of instruction), and their relationship with university administrators accordingly (Kim et al. [2018)](#page-19-6). As neoliberal steering nudges Chinese elite universities closer to their Western counterparts in term of research output and international prestige, an irreconcilable contradiction between academic freedom that underpins the success of Western universities and China's stringent ideological control arises. We, therefore, need to probe how WCU policy tries to strike a balance between 'not Western enough' and the danger of 'becoming too Western.'
#### *What can WPR offer?*
State and institutions' policymaking identified above resonates strongly with Yu's use of 'cross-field effects' theory to explain how the influences from economic, political, and other public policy fields coalesce changes into the education policy field (Yu [2018](#page-21-6)). Lingard, Rawolle and Taylor also argue that policies are relational in the sense that the formation of a global education policy field, which is seen as 'consisting of a site of contest between bureaucrats, policy advisors, politicians and "spin doctors"', is the result of the spread of logics of practice from other policy fields (Lingard, Rawolle, and Taylor [2005](#page-20-5), 11). Seen in this light, Chinese higher education internationalization policies are spillovers from other policy areas and thereby used as strategies to boost economic development, enhance national competitiveness, and increase international soft power. This view sidesteps investigation into how key concepts, such as WCU, assume their own
logic in producing 'problems' as problems of particular sorts (Bacchi and Goodwin [2016](#page-19-3)). Moreover, these theories – implicit in cross-field theory and explicit in policy field theory – privilege the role of policy entrepreneurs and competing interests of policymakers across policy arenas over the importance of policy text, which as '"instruments and effects" of discourse' (Ball [2015,](#page-19-7) 2), defines a system of conceptual possibilities within which we research.
Han and Ye ([2017](#page-19-8)) put forward the view that higher education policymaking in China should be studied from the lens of a policy network, in which policymakers, universities, and non-governmental professional groups all contribute to the process. Their central claim is that professional interest groups have over the years become important higher education policymakers in China. Again, they reduce the role of policy to actions addressing particular fixed problems, thereby emphasizing the role of agency of policy actors. This is a claim that cannot stand the test of time. In the past few years, the autonomy of universities and professional interest groups have shrunken dramatically. This volte-face is due precisely to the unique character of the Chinese political system they mention – the one-party state. Instead of studying the evershifting agency of actors, it may be more productive to investigate policymaking from a governmentality perspective, which involves understanding how internationalization policy is administered and how specific modes of subjectivity (such as 'professional group') are produced.
This study aims to offer a fresh perspective on the study of Chinese WCU policy in the following ways:
- (1) The object of policy analysis shifts from policy actors to policy documents, which are seen as discourses. - (2) The logic of investigation guiding policy analysis revolves around the representations of problems in policy documents as these texts create specific policy problems with particular meanings. - (3) The conceptual logic underpinning policy analysis shifts from governance to governmentality. Governance implies that actors have the power to negotiate, steer, and regulate in order to bring about an outcome, whereas governmentality sees power as sustained by processes and practices of administration.
## **Methodology**
### *WPR policy analysis*
In their pursuit of social inquiry, poststructuralists do not look for fixed 'truth,' but rather, seek to understand how things are constituted and how subjectivities are thereby created by discursive practices. Notably, poststructuralist theories emphasize the multiple and discursively constructed realities that are constantly produced in a setting for a particular audience and in a particular place. Thus, we can never know our world beyond our current concepts, knowledge, and discourse (Larsson [2018,](#page-19-9) 328). Accordingly, as a socially produced form of knowledge, discourse produces, establishes, and sets limits on what is possible to think, speak, and write. As a consequence, we perceive and live our world through the lens of discourse.
According to WPR, the constitution of a problem and its proposed solutions are inherent characteristics of policy discourses (Bacchi [2009](#page-18-3). Instead of engaging with how policymakers and stakeholders offer or perceive an interpretation of a problem, 'the analytic focus is on the conceptual underpinnings of identified governmental problematization or the forms of problematization in the policy documents' (Bacchi [2015,](#page-19-10) 3). WPR critically examines the ways problems are presented in policies. It questions the conventional view that policies are responses or reactions to problems that sit out of the policy. Instead, WPR adopts an ontological view that realities are produced in practices, where practices are the performances that are predicated upon and exercised within discourses. WPR is based on the premise that policy as proposed solutions contain implicit problem representations, that is, what a problem is considered to be. The way that problems and solutions are framed and represented indicates the logic of governance (Miller and Rose [2008](#page-20-6)). Government involves problematizing issues as 'problems', where problematizing, for poststructuralists, are ways of thinking that emerge from policy proposals rather than from people as agent (Bacchi [2012,](#page-18-4) 3). Problematization implies that some premises, presumptions, and representations are chosen over others while some representations are silenced. The goal of a WPR analysis is to explore these problematizations, thereby providing a framework for examining problem representation as specific forms of governmentality (Bacchi and Goodwin [2016,](#page-19-3) 28–29). It is a useful way of asking how this rendering of things problematic occurred and designating this inquiry as a process (Miller and Rose[ 2008](#page-20-6), 14). Bacchi's poststructural turn in policy analysis leads researchers to interrogate and rethink common forms of problematization in policy proposals (Bacchi [2012,](#page-18-4) 8).
For WPR, policy document is seen as a discourse, which is a knowledge system consisting of assumptions, presumptions and values, particular subjects, and subjectivities. We are governed by discourse. In this sense, policy is a technology of governmentality. Policy analysts' role is to deconstruct the problematizations through analyzing problem representations contained in policy documents, scrutinizing the premises, genealogy, dissemination channel, and subjectification effects of the said representations (Bacchi [2009](#page-18-3)).
The WPR policy analysis outlines six interrelated questions in [Table 1.](#page-6-0) These questions serve as just a guideline for analysis. Researchers can choose which question(s) to investigate, the order of investigation, or the format of investigation – question-by-question or integrated analysis. For this study, I will carry out the analysis in the following order: WPR's Questions 1, 2, 3, and 6 followed by Questions 4 and 5. The reason to put question 6 after question 3 is because these two questions are connected to the global context of WCU development while for questions 4 and 5 the focus is primarily on the Chinese context.
#### **Table 1. **WPR's six questions for analyzing policy documents.
Question 1 What is the problem represented to be in a specific policy or policies?
Question 2 What deep-seated presuppositions or assumptions underlie this representation of the 'problem' (problem representation)?
Question 3 How has this representation of the 'problem' come about?
Question 4 What is left unproblematic in this problem representation? Where are the silences? Can the 'problem' be conceptualized differently?
Question 5 What effects (discursive, subjectification, lived) are produced by this representation of the 'problem'? Question 6 How and where has this representation of the 'problem' been produced, disseminated, and defended? How has it been and/or how can it be disrupted and replaced?
### *Practical texts*
Foucault calls government regulations and decrees 'practical texts,' or 'prescriptive texts,' that are 'written for offering rules, opinions, and advice on how to behave as one should' ([1986](#page-19-11), 12– 13, cited in Bacchi [2012](#page-18-4), 2). WPR systemizes Foucault's suggestion that we should focus on 'practical texts' that 'made policy and wielded power' (Rabinow [2003](#page-20-7), 49). For WPR, policy texts are practical texts because they create a particular understanding of 'problems,' thereby providing ways of 'thinking and talking about our institutional ourselves, to ourselves and to others' (Ball [2015,](#page-19-7) 2), and of setting the limit on what is possible to speak or think.
Three policy document[s3](#page-18-5) were selected as practical texts. WCU is essentially a topdown policy. China's policymaking structure remains fundamentally hierarchical, and the 'territory' of policymaking remains firmly in the hand of the state. 'What is the problem represented to be' in the eyes of national government determines 'what is the problem represented to be' for all other actors. Therefore, two policies are chosen from the central government and its ministries that formally usher in this initiative. A policy from Tsinghua University is also included because it is the first and the only university in China that has 'achieved' WCU status after five years of 'construction', on 18 September 2020. Consequently, adding Tsinghua's document to the analysis is pertinent to understanding WCU representations. These documents are considered practical texts because they are prescriptive in offering rules on what universities and individuals can or should do in the pursuit of WCU. Moreover, these policies serve as levers to read other related policies, which are not listed here because of space limitation.
The title and year of the promulgation of these documents are as follows:
- Notice of the State Council on the Overall Plan for Promoting the Construction of World First-Class Universities and First-Class Disciplines, 2015 (hereafter, WCU Plan, 2015) [国务院:《统筹推进世界一流大学和一流学科建设总体方案的通知》] - Notice of the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance, and the National Development and Reform Commission on Printing and Distributing the Implementation Measures for Promoting the Construction of World First-Class Universities and First-Class Disciplines (Provisional), 2017 (hereafter, *WCU * Implementation Plan, 2017) [教育部, 财政部, 国家发展改革委:《统筹推进世界 一流大学和一流学科建设实施办法 (暂行) 的通知》] - Tsinghua University World-Class University Construction Plan, 2017 (hereafter, Tsinghua Plan, 2017) [清华大学:《清华大学一流大学建设高校建设方案》]
## **Analysis**
### *What is the problem represented to be in Chinese WCU (WPR's Question 1)*
The first entry for the WPR analysis begins with postulated solutions with which to work backwards through the policy texts to examine implicit problem representations, and how proposed solutions produce the 'problems' in policy proposals. The most prominent problem appears to be that an insufficient number of WCUs and world-class disciplines within universities is holding back on 'China's core national competitiveness' and the 'foundation of long-term development' and impeding the 'historical leap from a big country of higher education to a country of powerful higher education' (WCU Plan 2015,
Introduction). The prescribed solutions to achieve WCU are straightforward in the policy documents and can be broadly summarized as improvements in the following areas: 1) talents: world-class faculty and innovative students; 2) higher-level research and its commercialization; 3) international dimensions: exchanges and collaboration; 4) performance-linked funding for universities; and 5) cycles of a five-year plan for constructing WCUs starting in 2016 (WCU Plan 2015, 'construction tasks'[,4 ](#page-18-6)'reform tasks', 'supporting measures').
Therefore, the problem is represented to be a technical and managerial problem – human resources recruitment, funding for research output, and internationalization strategies – as well as a top-down organizational problem, which is state-led central planning. These problem representations are not entirely new but a continuation of past policy representations. For example, central and provincial governments poured nearly a total of 10 billion US dollars into the '985' project's two phases (1999–2003 and 2004– circa 2011), which benefited 34 and 39 universities, respectively (Huang [2015](#page-19-0), 208). As early as 2008, the Chinese government established the Thousand Talents Plan aimed at luring leading Chinese scientists, academics, and entrepreneurs in the West back to China with lavish compensation packages and promising career advancement opportunities (Barry and Kolata [2021](#page-19-12)). Seen from this perspective, the WCU policy is effectively 'putting new wine into old bottles', a Chinese metaphor, in this case describing new policy (WCU policy) being carried out in old forms. It is also striking that the evolution of Chinese aspirations for WCU from '211' to '985' to WCU plan did not bring about a gradual conceptual clarification of what world-class means. Throughout the policy documents, even a broad definition of world-class is nowhere to be found. It is no exaggeration to say that the problem representations in China's pursuit of WCU since the 1990s has been in a state of stasis.
Oxymoronically, 'world-class' has to be completely Chinese. To guide the attainment of WCU, political principles are also spelt out in the policies, which include 'comprehensively implementing the Party's educational policy, adhering to the socialist direction of running schools, and strengthening the Party's leadership over colleges and universities . . .. training successors of socialist cause and better serving socialist modernization' (WCU Plan 2015, 'overall principles'). In addition, Chinese WCU must be bearers and inheritors of 'excellent Chinese culture' and 'core socialist values' (WCU Plan 2015, 'construction tasks'). In this sense, another facet of WCU problem representation is that Chinese WCU has to be 'Chinese', that is, Western-like. The section below on effects of problem representation (WPR Question 5) will deal with these principles.
### *The Reification of WCU (WPR's Question 2)*
Question 2 asks which presuppositions or assumptions underlie the identified problem representation. This is the case with the notion of world-class. Chinese aspirations for WCU focuses on the tangible and measurable aspects of 'excellence', which primarily include outstanding facilities, well-known academics, high-ranked research output, and recognition beyond national boundaries (Douglass [2016)](#page-19-13). The engines for achieving excellence are competition, entrepreneurial spirits, and performance-linked government funding. The characterizations of WCU are formulaic and parochial, simplifying the
multifarious and complex nature of the notion of world-class to a few basic metrics, while turning a blind eye to historicity, roots, and other hard-to-measure qualities. These representations have been discussed in detail in the literature. I will give more space to the representation of attainability of WCU through top-down planning.
Five-year plans result from the simplistic understanding of WCU and the Chinese state's habitus of planning. When the Chinese Communist Party (the Party) founded the People's Republic of China in 1949, China adopted the Soviet Union's model of a central command economy. One defining feature of this model is its Five-Year Plan, for which an input-output analysis is employed to calculate the targets for each industry across five annual plans (Perkins [2015](#page-20-8), 43). After transitioning from a full-command economy to a market economy with Chinese characteristics, five-year plans are still being drawn up, albeit only for 'the general direction of government policy and the government investment program' (Perkins [2015](#page-20-8), 53). WCU is such a national plan that exhibits the logic of accomplishing a national strategical goal by top-down policy design and through directed implementation with generous resource allocation. Article 15[5](#page-18-7) of the WCU Implementation Plan (2017) stipulates that the funding for the construction of WCUs is supported by the central government. In 2019, China's 30 wealthiest elite universities recorded annual expenditures over US$1 billion – a figure surpassed only in the United States (Hartley and Jarvis [2021,](#page-19-14) 9).
As with all the central planning, the goals are spelt out unequivocally at the outset: by 2020, some universities and disciplines become world-class and some disciplines become world leading, and by 2030, more universities and disciplines become worldclass and world leading, with a noticeable increase in the comprehensive quality of HE (WCU Plan 2015, 'overall goals' section). Tsinghua University's self-certified worldclass status demonstrates the self-fulfilling prophecy effect of national planning. Had it (or other universities) not become world-class in 2020, it would have meant that planning had failed.
### *Linking economic neoliberalism and knowledge-based economy to WCU (WPR's * *Question 3)*
The goal of Question 3 is to 'reflect on the specific development and decisions (the nondiscursive practices) that contribute to the formation of identified problem representations' (Bacchi [2009,](#page-18-3) 10). Genealogy in WPR is not a detailed chronological history of origins. . I will specifically investigate a global movement for the following reasons:
- (1) WCU is inherently situated within a broader context of globalization and the spread of global neoliberalism. - (2) The WCU movement represents a worldwide trend toward isomorphism, hence 'should not be studied merely from the national point of view but needs to include the possibility of transnational organization fields and international pressures for convergence with those fields. We need to identify the international factors that create the pressures for conformity and promote the adoption of global modes' (Beerkens [2008,](#page-19-15) 24).
[FIGURE: see A2.R57_fig07.jpg]
(3) WCU is not a Chinese indigenous concept. On the contrary, it is a concept developed in the West and modeled on Western elite universities. Hence, it is vital to bridge the gap between its gestation in the West and germination in China.
The reform and opening u[p6 ](#page-18-8)undertaken by Deng Xiaoping represented 'the construction of a particular kind of market economy that increasingly incorporates neoliberal elements interdigitated with authoritarian centralized control' (Harvey [2007](#page-19-16), 120). In searching for an alternative to replace the Soviet model of higher education, China looked toward the United States, which provided a model and a neoliberal justification (Zhao and Zhu [2010](#page-21-7), 118). The idea for WCU began to surface in Chinese policies in the early 2000s, during which the role of Chinese higher education internationalization was increasingly tied with China's economic competitiveness in the global market (Wang and Seddon [2014](#page-21-3)).
Within Chinese higher education, the concept of WCU was germinated in the context of knowledge-based economy (KBE). World Bank's *The 1998/99 World Development Report: * *Knowledge for Development *(World Bank [1999](#page-21-8)) proposed KBE as the developmental framework for developing countries to catch up with developed economies. At the behest of the Chinese government, the World Bank sought to address how China could ensure its sustained economic development in the 21st century and advance its position in the global knowledge revolution by upgrading institutional reforms, education, and R&D (Dahlman and Aubert [2001)](#page-19-17). According to the World Bank's *China and the Knowledge Economy: * *Seizing the 21st Century*, top Chinese universities should be the major actors in China's transformation into a KBE, training future thinkers and leaders and remaining actively and directly involved in generating and applying knowledge for economic growth (Dahlman and Aubert [2001](#page-19-17), 132). According to Hu Angang, the director of the Institute for Contemporary China Studies at Tsinghua University, many ideas in the report were incorporated into China's national 10th Five-Year Plan and the 10th Five-Year Special Development Project Planning in education, science, and technology (Hu[ 2002,](#page-19-18) 4). The enablers of KBE were also evident in the World Bank's 2007 policy working paper, *China and the Knowledge Economy: * *Challenges and Opportunities *(Zeng and Wang [2007](#page-21-9)), which identified 'weak indigenous innovation capacity, low quality of tertiary education, its inadequate relevance to the market', and 'poor linkages' between government's research and development (R&D) institutes, businesses, and universities as impediments to a knowledge economy (Zeng and Wang [2007](#page-21-9), 20–21).
In the West, the concept of KBE is an 'empirical description' and 'quasi-benchmarking of central features of existing economies', the harnessing and improvement of which can enhance competitiveness (Jessop [2008](#page-19-19), 25). In contrast, China in the 2000s aspired to build a knowledge economy that could support sustained economic growth at home and integrate itself into the global economic network.
Yang also noted that in the 1990s and early 2000s, other international organizations, such as the World Trade Organization, also 'lent' its ideology of market fundamentalism in the form of 'expert consultants to the Chinese higher education sector' (Yang [2010](#page-21-10)). KBE is inseparable from the neoliberal imaginary, wherein knowledge is considered a new form of competitive capital whose production is linked to economic fundamentals. In order to unleash the competitive potential, neoliberal developmentalism advocates a global economic order, national strategic reorientation of higher education, and
institutional and individual performance-linked self-regulation. Around the same period, marketization and decentralization took place alongside higher education massification in China. Some watershed reforms included charging student university fees, the creation of internal competition mechanisms within and between universities, and creating feegenerating courses and degrees (Mok [2000)](#page-20-9). They paved way for the emergence of a WCU project.
The WCU policy is regarded as a corrective to the problems inherent in its precursors – the '211' and '985' projects. One of their flaws was their 'identity rigidification' (another way of saying elite universities should not settle on their prestigious status and should strive for more competition), and also 'lack of competition, duplication and overlapping of research'; it is therefore hoped that WCUs can 'consolidate resources and be innovative' (WCU Plan 2015, 'Introduction'). The antidotes recommended are 'establishing and improving performance evaluation mechanism and actively adopting third-party evaluation' because these measures can improve the 'scientificity and credibility' of the quality assurance system (WCU Plan 2015, 'strengthening performance, dynamic support'). Furthermore, funding based on evaluation can enhance the efficiency of potential WCUs (WCU Plan 2015, 'strengthening performance, dynamic support').
### *University ranking: movers and shakers of WCU (WPR's Question 6)*
Question 6 takes refers to the dissemination and production of particular problem representations. Global rankings are the norm of the world-class status despite that 'rankings have installed a crisp global homogenization with clear-cut drivers of policy and institutional strategy' (Marginson [2018](#page-20-10), 32–35). Rankings offer a false pretense that the 'excellence' of WCU can be demonstrated by some statistics. The power of rankings is derived from the misconceived equivalence between a university's position in rankings and its 'measurable' scale of excellence.
A study on WCU would not be incomplete without examining the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU), the brainchild of the Centre for World-class Universities (CWCU) of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, established in 2002[.7 ](#page-18-9)CWCU was designated as a strategic research unit by China's MOE in 2005 to recognize its 'long tradition of providing high-quality consultation reports to the Chinese government on strategies for building world-class universities and other science and technology policies' (MOE[ 2005](#page-20-11)). Liu, CWCU's founder and director, explicitly stated that 'to quantitatively analyze the position of Chinese universities in the world university system and find out their gap with world-class universities, it is necessary to quantitatively compare, and rank based on internationally comparable indicators' (Liu, Cheng, and Liu [2005](#page-20-12), 10). ARWU has given the Chinese governments and universities a roadmap to 'excellence,' significantly altering the direction of higher education policymaking in terms of tools, purpose, and outcome. Ranking is conceived as a 'policy instrument' (Salmi and Saroyan [2007)](#page-20-13) that can help China's elite universities become world leading.
The CWCU has been organizing biennial conferences on various themes of the concept of WCU since 2005 in Shanghai. The conferences have brought prominent academics, university presidents, policymakers, government officials, and CEOs of higher education commercial companies together. The lists have included Simon Marginson (Oxford University), Marijk van der Wende (university of Utrecht), William Kirby
(Harvard University), the presidents of Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München in Germany and the University of Virginia in the US, former World Bank policy advisor Jamil Salmi, the director of the European Centre for Higher Education, and the chief executive of the Higher Education Funding Council for England, to name a few. These individuals are eminent movers and shakers of the global movement of WCU. Their participation and ideation shape the form, content, and direction of the concept of WCU. [Table 2 ](#page-12-0)lists the themes of past conferences. From 2005 to 2019, we have witnessed a gradual concretization of the definitions and conceptual dimensions of WCU as a conceptualization, ranging from the characteristics and goals of WCU, and national strategies to achieve WCU, to the impact of WCU on the global common good and globalization.
After firmly establishing itself as one of the global authorities in international rankings, ARWU rolled out the *Best Chinese Universities Ranking *and *Best Chinese Subjects * *Ranking *in 2015 and 2017, respectively. With the publication of these two rankings, we see a global ranking, along with its metrics, projected onto domestic higher education. For domestic rankings, the national, Asian, and world rankings are juxtaposed in the institutional profile of a university, as shown in [Figure 1](#page-14-0), allowing users to promptly detect the standings of a university in each ranking category, as well as the potential for improvement. Further down the profile, the positions of all disciplines of the said university in the discipline world ranking is listed. These moves directly benchmark Chinese universities against their own and their peers' global standings. When ARWU was first devised, WCU was a distant goal for China. However, in fewer than two decades, flagship Chinese universities have begun moving from the periphery to the center of global higher education. ARWU has been successful in its effort to localize the concept of WCU and imprint it on Chinese universities.

### *Silenced knowledge in Chinese WCU (WPR's Question 4)*
The marginalization of a particular representation in the policy text can also be considered silencing because it does not get the voice it deserves. In the two central policy documents, the word 'science' (in the sense of technology or 'hard' sciences) appeared 29 times, while 'humanities' made no appearance at all and 'social science' appeared three times, two of which were 'China's philosophy and social science system' (WCU Plan 2015, 'construction tasks' and WCU Implementation Plan 2017, Article 5) and one of which was about 'philosophy and social science research providing effective support for solving major theoretical and practical problems in economic and social development' (WCU Implementation Plan 2017, Article 7). In the Tsinghua document, 'science' appeared 37 times, whereas 'humanities' and 'social science' each appeared eight times. The marginalization of humanities and social sciences (HSS) in policy discourse is noteworthy.
Since the WCU profile is normed by global rankings, institutions fashion their strategies to maximize their rankings in physical sciences/engineering and life sciences/ medicine – two areas that rankings prize the most (Marginson [2018,](#page-20-10) 32). Furthermore, science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) subjects have increasingly become a transnational collaborative endeavor post-1990 (Marginson [2021a](#page-20-14), 9). As a result, STEM subjects, in contradistinction to HSS, involve more international collaboration and output in the international arena. This means greater visibility and impact. As [Figure 2](#page-15-0) shows, in the development of Chinese WCU, the monochromatic stress on the development of STEM subjects echoes a widespread incantation of truism that equates achievements in STEM with world-class status.
Interestingly, the success of China's single-minded pursuit of STEM subjects as manifested by the continual rise of its flagship universities in rankings has reinforced, instead of disrupting, WCU problem representations, such as the attainability of WCU and the paramount importance of STEM. Thanks to the combined effects of national funding for sciences, the strategic emphasis of some science disciplines, and the internationalization strategy of collaboration with global partners, China is now the largest producer of papers and number one in parts of STEM physical sciences (Marginson [2021b](#page-20-15)). If the number of high citation papers in global science is taken as a measure of excellence, Chinese flagship universities have unequivocally achieved world-class status (Marginson[ 2021b)](#page-20-15); as pointed out in the Tsinghua document, Tsinghua's continued rise in rankings results from the sustained improvement of its 'comprehensive strength and international influence' (Tsinghua Plan 2017, Chapter 1, section 2). If we look from this lopsided vantage point, Tsinghua's self-certification of WCU seems justified.
The negligence of HSS in China's WCU policy is only partially attributable to China's prioritized catching up in STEM subjects or the English-language barrier faced by many Chinese HSS academics. The fundamental reason for marginalization has to do with the ideological strictures of China's political system, which dictates what can or should be researched. STEM researchers can carry out unfettered research, while HSS researchers have to 'dance in the cage' (Yang, Vidovich, and Currie [2007)](#page-21-11). An examination of the policy documents shows that HSS is always articulated in the context of socialist ideology or the so-called special HSS system with Chinese characteristics. In other words, these policies dictate that science should be global, but Chinese HSS is exclusively Chinese.

As a result, the 'great leap forward' of Chinese HSS has been happening predominantly on the domestic front and in line with pro-party ideology. Xi Jinping ushered in a new era of ideological control when he came to power in 2012. There are currently 18 centers – including one at Tsinghua – devoted to the study of Xi Jinping Thought. Three areas out of 23 social science disciplines funded by the National Social Science Fund saw a marked increase in funding at the expense of disciplines, such as economics, law, literature, and philosophy. These three disciplines are 1) Marxism & scientific socialism; 2) ethnic studies; and 3) Party history & Party building (Thomas [2020](#page-21-12)).
The growth of China's global science research and ideology-driven domestic HSS research are the two sides of the same WCU coin. Globally, the meteoric rise of Chinese capacity in sciences have overshadowed, if not legitimized, the lackluster performance in HSS. China is determined to replicate the success of Western elite universities in STEM subjects. At that time, it wants to appropriate that success to buttress a higher education system that is undergirded by ideology. China may have set a bad example for aspiring universities in developing countries by providing a distorted representation of what
WCUs can look like. Moreover, we live in a world where democratic foundations of societies have been increasingly challenged, if not threatened, and where our future becomes uncertain owing to factors such as climate change and the Covid-19 pandemic; the marginalization of a global-minded HSS is detrimental to our collective capability to confront these challenges.
### *Effects of WCU representations (WPR's Question 5)*
Question 5 investigates the effects that follow from particular problem representations. Specific problem representations produce specific subjectification effects on institutions and individuals (Bacchi [2009](#page-18-3), 15). Individuals in Chinese universities are affected by WCU on two fronts. They share a similar kind of discursive, lived, and subjectification effects with their Western counterparts brought about by the neoliberal representation of WCU. For example, the lived effect of neoliberal higher education means academics have to align their work with the economy and make education an efficient and competitive service sector. They are, consequently, subjected to performativity, accountability, and self-responsibilization.
China's quest for WCU is underpinned and distinguished by its political system – a Marxist-Leninist one-party state. We now turn to the principles identified at the beginning (in second part of Q1). For designated Chinese WCUs, they are required to be 'inheritors of Chinese traditional culture' (WCU Implementation Plan 2017, Article 7), and 'obey Party's leadership' (WCU Implementation Plan 2017, Article 25). Their foremost duty is 'promoting research that enhances national interests' (WCU Implementation Plan 2017, Article 5). Discursively, these policy documents generate a 'truth regime' wherein the binaries of party loyalty/party disloyalty and traditional/ Western cultures become opposing and irreconcilable. Political loyalty and adherence to 'traditional culture' become the unquestionable truths even though these key concepts are extremely ambiguous.
In addition to identifying themselves as researchers and learners, faculties and students also become political subjects by 'eliciting certain behaviours, feelings, and views' (Bacchi[ 2009](#page-18-3), 93), such as strictly toeing the Party's ideological line (Tsinghua Plan 2017, chapter 1, section 2), or adhering to Core Socialist Values and striving to become 'red' professionals who support socialism and serve national interests, such as socialist modernization (Tsinghua Plan 2017, chapter 1, section 2). Such subjectification stands in sharp contrast to the above-mentioned neoliberal subjects. 'Red and expert' as a concept that rationalizes intellectuals' subservience to party ideology has been popular since the Maoist era, and WCU policy seems to reinforce this subjectification.
Lived effects are material consequences that individuals have to face in their daily life. Ideology education is an indispensable part of 'knowledge' in Chinese universities, accounting for 10% of the undergraduate curriculum (Jiang [2018)](#page-19-20). In December 2017, MOE issued a policy document stating that 'ideological and political performance' would be the single most heavily weighted criterion in the evaluation of faculties. The subjectification of individuals takes place not just at the political level. Designating individuals as inheritors of Chinese culture or successors of socialist modernization and core socialist values gives them a false sense of entitlement, purpose, agency, and even emancipation. The mystification of these concepts, aided by relentless repetition and
inculcation, portrays a self-evident common sense, whereby individuals complicitly subordinate themselves to give allegiance to the state's hegemonic project (Gramsci [1971](#page-19-21)).
## **Conclusion**
Conventionally, policy analysis has followed an interpretivist tradition wherein the agency of people is emphasized. At the policy formulation level, researchers of Chinese education policy try to understand the policy rationales and agendas or the coordination of interests among policy actors (e.g. Han and Ye [2017)](#page-19-8). At the institutional level, researchers focus on the strategies adopted by universities' management in their responses for calls to build WCU (e.g. Pan 2016). Ethnographic studies are carried out to explore the impact of the neoliberal dimensions of WCU policy on academic staff and students, such as the pressure to publish in international journals (e.g. Xu[ 2020)](#page-21-4). In other words, the focus of these analyses is on how people engage with and interpret policies. In contrast, in Foucault-influenced poststructuralism, 'the analytical focus is on the conceptual underpinnings of identified governmental problematizations . . . rather than on social actors as problematizing' (Bacchi[ 2015](#page-19-10), 3). This directs researchers' attention away from the purposeful and agentic social actors to 'critical interrogation of the problematizations within existing policies' (Bacchi [2015](#page-19-10), 4). As a form of poststructural discourse analysis, WPR views policy document as the policy discourse that produces the very problem it is meant to solve because policy is a proposal of what to do with a 'problem'. Policy, thus, contains implicit problem representations. WPR aims to explore these representations and open up the analysis to a critique of their presuppositions, site of dissemination and effects.
This study seeks to complement existing scholarly work on Chinese WCU by providing a governmentality perspective. Analyzing WCU policy from a governmentality angle means paying attention to the specific practices involved in the governing of WCU and ways in which these practices establish a certain rationality and constitute particular kinds of subjects. Although the meaning of WCU is never clearly spelt out, as a policy tool, it problematizes its policy territory by proposing what a Chinese WCU should look like and what can be done to achieve it. This paper demonstrates that WCU is represented as a technical, managerial, and organizational issue. Such presentations are inherently and implicitly premised on the narrow conception of what constitutes WCU, thereby objectifying it in terms of research out and internationalization among others. Coupled with China's central planning tradition and mentality, this objectification is veered with a semblance of obtainability within a predetermined time frame. Problem representations do not appear out of thin air. They have a history. China's pursuit of WCU should first and foremost be contextualized with the global movement of neoliberal higher education.
This article also draws attention to the central role played by Shanghai ranking as a normative tool and measurement to disseminate the idea that WCU is measurable and with the right ingredients, they can be achieved. Shanghai Ranking calls the proposition that Chinese universities are the periphery of global higher education (Xu [2020)](#page-21-4) into question. A country in the periphery can initiate a scheme that those at the center have also to play along. As said above, the subjectification of academics is usually researched
under a neoliberal framework. This paper highlights the discursive, subjectification, and lived effects of Chinese academics and students who have researched and studied 'within the entire moral landscape of the nation and society' within the parameters deemed acceptable by the Party (Lin and Trevaskes [2019](#page-20-16), 45). In a nutshell, WPR reminds us, researchers, to question how a policy produces rather than solves problems. We should critically question rather than adopt what is being represented in a policy.
